question: Which of the following can be blocked by atropine, a muscarinic receptor blocker?

options.opa: Increased blood pressure caused by nicotine
options.opb: Increased skeletal muscle strength caused by neostigmine, an acetycholine esterase inhibitor
options.opc: Bradycardia caused by infusion of acetylcholine

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Atropine" -> "blocks muscarinic receptors" -> "prevents acetylcholine from binding to muscarinic receptors in the heart" -> "prevents slowing of heart rate" -> "does not affect bradycardia caused by acetylcholine" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Atropine" -> "blocks muscarinic receptors" -> "does not interact with nicotinic receptors" -> "does not block effects of nicotine on blood pressure" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Atropine" -> "blocks muscarinic receptors" -> "does not affect skeletal muscle strength" -> "neostigmine increases acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions, which are nicotinic receptors" -> "does not block increased skeletal muscle strength caused by neostigmine" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Atropine" -> "blocks muscarinic receptors" -> "does not block effects mediated by nicotinic receptors" -> "none of the listed options are solely mediated by muscarinic receptors" -> "does not block all of these" -> 95%
analysis: Atropine is a muscarinic receptor antagonist that blocks the action of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors. Option A involves nicotine, which primarily acts on nicotinic receptors, not muscarinic receptors, so atropine would not be effective. Option B involves neostigmine, which increases skeletal muscle strength by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction, primarily affecting nicotinic receptors, thus atropine would not block this effect. Option C, bradycardia caused by acetylcholine, directly involves muscarinic receptors in the heart, where atropine can effectively block the action of acetylcholine, preventing bradycardia.
